Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check Principle 2: Choose a safe landing site before entering the water (p. 57).
Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check Principle 3: In exceptional cases, such as in a steep-sided quarry, you mayboth need help from others onshore (p. 57).
Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check Principle 4: When landing a conscious victim, lower your legs to check the water depth if you can do so without causing the victim to lose support (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): Natural bodies of water can be shallow for long distances from shore (p. 57).
Step 2 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): It may be easier to walkthrough shallow water than it is to swim (p. 57).
Step 3 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): If the victim is exhausted, cold, or hastrouble with footing, help him or her ashore using a shallow-waterassist (p. 57).
Step 4 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): While standing at the person's side, help him or her to stand and to place one arm around your neck and across your shoulder (p. 57).

Step 3 (Importance of Avoiding Contact): For short distances, you can aid a cooperative tired personswimming on his or her stomach by swimming alongside andgrasping the upper arm (p. 59).
Step 4 (Importance of Avoiding Contact): If the person is trying a restful backstroke, a single armpittow is appropriate (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: Contact Assists for Active Victims: If an active victim will not follow you to shore, back offand wait (p. 60).
Contact Assists for Active Victims Principle 2: The person may become more cooperative as he orshe tires (p. 60).

Contact Assists for Active Victims Principle 4: Stay close enough to place the victim in a tow if it becomes necessary (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): In rare cases you may need to provide assistance to someone bysupporting them without a flotation device (p. 60).
Step 2 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): One such circumstance is if you and others are caught in a rip current and some of the party become increasingly tired trying to swim (p. 60).
Step 3 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): For short distances, you can aid a cooperative tired personswimming on his or her stomach by swimming alongside andgrasping the upper arm (p. 60).
Step 4 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): If the person is trying a restful backstroke, a single armpittow is appropriate (p. 60).

pamphlet_excerpts: Management of a spinal injury: Diving into shallow or unclear water is unsafe and foolish (p. 85).
Management of a spinal injury Principle 2: Thediver risks spinal injury, permanent paralysis, or death (p. 85).
Management of a spinal injury Principle 3: In pools, most diving injuries happen in shallow water but also can occurif the diver hits another swimmer or a diving board (p. 85).
Management of a spinal injury Principle 4: In lakes and rivers, diving injuries are caused by misjudging thedepth of the water or hitting rocks or trees unseen from the surface (p. 85).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Management of a spinal injury): At beaches, lunging intowaves or falling off a board can cause spinal injury when a wave slams the victiminto the bottom (p. 85).
Step 2 (Management of a spinal injury): If you notice anyone dive into the water and float immobile to the surface, call for help immediately (p. 85).
Step 3 (Management of a spinal injury): Head, neck, and spinalinjuries are extremely serious and are best handled by trainedpersonnel with special equipment (p. 85).
Step 4 (Management of a spinal injury): If trained and equippedpersonnel are not immediatelyavailable, your job is to maintain the person in a faceup stable position until help (p. 85).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Knowledge of resuscitation procedure): Recall that some victims who need rescue may be injured (p. 79).

Step 2 (Knowledge of resuscitation procedure): If you notice the victim is bleeding, apply direct pressure to the wounds as soon as possible after you provide support and check that the person (p. 79).
Step 3 (Knowledge of resuscitation procedure): Various preexisting medical conditions may lead to distressin the water (p. 79).
Step 4 (Knowledge of resuscitation procedure): The first priority is to support the victim to prevent respiratory arrest from drowning (p. 79).
